logistic.title: Logistic regression: train, then predict
logistic.caption: Start with labelled messages, turn them into word-count vectors, and let LogisticRegression.fit learn the weights. The small training set below makes every input visible.
logistic.challenge: Choose a new message. Follow its vector through the learned weights to the predicted class.

flow.title: How logistic regression learns and predicts

stages.title: 1 · Learn weights from the training vectors and labels

nodes.label: Fit once on the six training messages
nodes.text: A weight is learned for each column. Positive weights support spam; negative weights support ham. These numbers come from fitting the training data above.

stages.title: 2 · Convert the new message into the same columns

nodes.label: New message → word-count vector
nodes.text: Use the training vocabulary. Other words do not create new columns.

stages.title: 3 · Apply the learned weights, then predict

nodes.label: Calculate the score
nodes.text: Only words present in this message contribute.

nodes.label: Convert the score to a probability
nodes.text: Choose the class with the larger probability. The model stays fixed when you change the new message.

flow.caption: The training labels teach LR the weights. Prediction reuses those weights on a new word-count vector.

knn.title: KNN: find neighbours, then vote
knn.caption: KNN keeps the labelled training vectors. For a new message, calculate distances, take the closest k, then count their labels. We keep only prize and class to make these vectors easy to inspect.
knn.challenge: Choose a message and follow the distance ranking. Changing k changes which training messages vote.

flow.title: How KNN finds neighbours and predicts

nodes.label: Training uses no word coefficients
nodes.code:
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
model = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k, metric="cosine")
model.fit(X_toy, y_toy)
nodes.text: KNN keeps the vectors and labels shown above; prediction looks up nearby examples.

stages.title: 2 · Represent the new message and calculate distances

nodes.label: Use the same two word columns
nodes.text: Cosine distance compares directions: 0 means the same direction, and smaller means closer.

nodes.label: Rank all training messages by distance
nodes.text: ✓ marks the closest k messages selected to vote. Ties can depend on training order.

stages.title: 3 · Count the selected labels, then predict

nodes.label: Each selected neighbour gets one vote
nodes.text: Uniform voting uses the labels, not a weighted sum of word coefficients. Change k and follow which messages join the vote.

flow.caption: New message → same feature columns → distances → closest k labels → majority vote. The full SMS model below uses TF–IDF instead of this small count example.
